newsitem.title: USA: NYNEX, AT&T sign N.Y. interconnection pact.
newsitem.headline: NYNEX, AT&T sign N.Y. interconnection pact.

text.p: NYNEX Corp said Tuesday it had reached an interconnection pact that further opens its local phone market by allowing long distance provider AT&T Corp to begin offering local phone service in New York State.
Suzanne Berman, a spokeswoman for AT&T, the nation's leading long distance company, confirmed that an agreement had been reached.

The deal was reached after being submitted to arbitration before the New York State Public Service Commission. The deal has been signed by NYNEX and AT&T and submitted for Commission approval within 30 days, NYNEX said.
Interconnection refers to the process whereby the existing local exchange carrier such as NYNEX opens up its local service network to other companies.
AT&T's spokeswoman said it was the first deal AT&T had reached in the NYNEX's six-state service region.

AT&T has signed and won approval from state regulators for 15 such deals with Baby Bell local service companies in other states. Bell Atlantic is the sole local exchange carrier yet to reach such a deal with AT&T, the spokeswoman said.

Bell Atlantic and NYNEX are awaiting final approval from U.S. regulators on their proposed merger, announced last year, which would form the nation's largest local phone company in terms of revenues, and would stretch from Maine to Virginia.
Separately, NYNEX said it had agreed to a draft interconnection deal with MCI Communications Corp.
MCI recently withdrew a complaint charging NYNEX with negotiating in bad faith during previous interconnection talks by the two parties.
An MCI spokeswoman confirmed that such a deal had been reached.

NYNEX said the deal has been turned over to another arbitration team, which is expected to reach final decision on the details and submit a complete MCI interconnection pact to the Public Service Commission for approval shortly after the AT&T agreement.
MCI spokeswoman Julianne Forrest said MCI already offers some local services to business customers in New York City.
MCI plans to expand to offer business and some residential services in the suburbs of New York by the year-end, she said.

Opening its network to competition from other local service providers is a key requirement set forth by federal law before NYNEX will be allowed to seek regulatory approval to enter the long-distance market in its home territory.
NYNEX said it has now signed 34 land-line based interconnection deals and 39 wireless pacts in the six-state Northeast region in which it operates.

NYNEX has been working with the New York Public Service Commission since February to finalize a draft application for long-distance entry in New York. The application is expected to be filed later this year with the U.S. Federal Communications Commission.

Regarding the interconnection agreement with NYNEX, AT&T vice president Michael Morrissey said in a statement that the deal was just "one more step" toward full competition, but that key issues remain.

"Today's rulings are part of a larger agreement about terms and conditions (for entering the N.Y. local service business) but do not resolve the issue of non-competitive costs competitors face when entering local markets," he said.

After trading listlessly throughout the day Tuesday, AT&T stock gained on the news, which was released at about 1515 EDT/1915 GMT. AT&T stock closed up 3/4 at 34-1/4 on volume of more than 4.4 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
NYNEX closed up 1/8 on the day at 52-5/8. MCI stock closed at 38-1/8, unchanged from the previous day's close.
One Wall Street analyst was surprised by the sudden surge in AT&T trading following the news.

"Anyone who was not expecting AT&T to get an interconnection agreement in New York State was foolish," said Schroeder Wertheim analyst Phil Sirlin, who said N.Y. state regulators are aggressive advocates of local competition.
Sirlin has a sell rating on AT&T stock.
-- Eric Auchard, New York newsdesk, 212-859-1736
